title: Women in Zen: Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: The talk highlights the importance of recognizing and honoring the contributions of female monastics throughout Buddhist history, who played a significant role in spreading the Buddha's teachings and creating a rich tradition of monastic life for women. The Therigata, an ancient collection of poems, preserves the voices and experiences of early Buddhist nuns who achieved enlightenment through their practice, offering profound insights into the transformative power of the Dharma regardless of gender or social status. These women's stories show that true freedom can be found by letting go of attachments and embracing impermanence, a message that is still relevant today for all practitioners.

sentences.text: Good evening.
It's wonderful to be here, especially since I'm talking about a subject that is dear to my heart, and that is women in Buddhist sanghas.
As we will discover, it was not always very rosy, probably still isn't today, but we're making progress.
I brought some books that I enjoy on the subject, and please feel free to take a look at them before you walk out.
There's a couple of books I'm missing, but I lend out books all the time, and sometimes they don't quite find their way back.
So, women's lineages.
Years ago, a student came to my teacher, Zoketsu Norman Fischer, in Dokusan.
She was weeping.
She said that every morning in the monastery, we all chant the names of the ancestors.
And weeping, she asked, where are the women?
Where are the women ancestors?
This is how our women's lineage came to be.
Many Zen teachers worked together, and in October 2010, the document was approved by SCBA, which is the American Association of Buddhist Teachers.
While the men's lineage is linear, the women's lineage is not.
I just want to unfold this and let you take a look at it.
This is the women's lineage, and this is part of my ordination documents, but I would still like to hand it around, but please treat it nicely.
The design of the circle is showing the names of female ancestors.
This list is incomplete.
History has not been kind to women.
Their accomplishments have often been disregarded, the history deleted or rewritten, their existence denied.
It's interesting, though, that some of the male ancestors may actually have been female.
When their successors wrote the history, they got a little sex change to make it more acceptable.
The establishment of this women's lineage is a step in the right direction to at least recognize the existence of the female in the Dharma.
Also, writing this Dharma talk, I have come to realize that I have neglected to give my students this important document.
We'll clean that up, and I will be sending out, and handing out, this document to my students who have done Chukai with me.
So I'm working to take care of this mistake, and I'm grateful and happy that Soto Zen in this place and time is inclusive.
As a gender, though, we had somewhat of a rough start.
This is the beginning of the women's sangha, from the book, The Life of Buddha.
I have slightly edited the passage to shorten it a bit.
*The Buddha, the Blessed One, was living among the Sakyans in Nikrodas Park at Kapilavastu.
Mahapachapari Gautami went to him.
She paid homage and stood at one side.
Then she said, Lord, it would be good if women could obtain the going forth from the house life into homelessness in the Dharma and discipline declared by the Perfect One.
The Buddha replied, Enough, Gautami, do not ask for the going forth from the house life into homelessness for women.
In the Dharma and discipline declared by the Perfect One, she asked a second and a third time, and she was refused.
Then she thought, the Blessed One does not allow it, and she was sad and unhappy.*
*She paid homage to the Blessed One and departed, keeping him on her right.
The Buddha leaves the place where he was born, and he wanders on.
However, Mahapachapari Gautami cut her hair off, and she put on a yellow robe.
With a number of Sakyan women, she set out for Thubesali, where the Buddha stayed.
On arrival, she went to the hall, [unclear: "was the pointed roof in the great wood"], and she stood there outside the porch.
Her feet were swollen, her limbs covered with dust.
She was sad, with tears on her face and sobbing.
As she stood thus, the Venerable Ananda saw her.*
*He asked her, Gautami, why are you standing outside the porch like this?
Lord Ananda, it is because the Blessed One does not allow the going forth for women in the Dharma and discipline declared by the Perfect One.
Then Gautami, wait here till I ask the Blessed One about this.

The Venerable Ananda went to the Blessed One and told him what had happened, and he said, Lord, it would be good if women might obtain the going forth from the house life into homelessness in the Dharma and discipline declared by the Perfect One.
Enough, Ananda.
Do not ask for the going forth from the house life.
Ananda asked a second and a third time and was refused.*

*Ananda said, Lord, are women capable after going forth from the house life into homelessness in the Dharma and discipline declared by the Perfect One, of realizing the fruit of stream entry, or once return, or non-return, or arhatship?
The Buddha replied, they are, Ananda.

If that is so, Lord, then since Mahapajapati Gautami has been exceedingly helpful to the Blessed One, when his mother's sister, she was his nurse, his foster mother, his giver of milk, she suckled the Blessed One when his own mother died.
Since that is so, Lord, would it be good if women could obtain the going forth?
The Buddha replied, Ananda, if Mahapajapati Gautami accepts eight capital points that will count as her full admission.
These are the eight points.*
*A bhikkhuni*, bhikkhuni means nun, *who has been admitted even a hundred years must pay homage to, get up for, reverentially salute, and respectfully greet a bhikkhu*, a monk, *admitted that day.
A bhikkhuni must not spend the rains in a place where there are no bhikkhus.

Every half month, bhikkhuni should expect two things from the Sangha of bhikkhus: the appointment of the Uposatha day of observance each half month and visit for exhortation.* So Uposatha is when we do the refuges and we confess all our ancient twisted karma and go through the precepts.
*At the end of the rains, a bhikkhuni must invite criticism of both Sanghas in the three instances.*
*That is, whether anything improper in her conduct has been seen, heard, or suspected.
When a bhikkhuni has committed a grave offense, she must do the penance before both Sanghas.
A probationer who seeks admission must do so from both Sanghas and after training in the six things for two years.
A bhikkhuni must not find fault with or abuse a bhikkhu in any manner at all.
From today onwards, it is not allowed for bhikkhunis to address discourses to bhikkhus, but it is allowed for bhikkhus to address bhikkhunis.
These eight things are to be honored, respected, revered, and venerated, and they are not to be transgressed as long as life lasts.
If Maha Pachapati Gotami accepts these eight capital points, that will count as her full admission.
She did, and she was happy.*
That's at least what this Pali Canon says.
In spite of the additional rules placed on the nuns, the inclusion of women in the Sangha was a groundbreaking moment.
Not only in the history of Buddhism, but also in the history of religious and social equality.
While the Buddha's decision to admit women came with restrictions, it also affirmed the women's ability to pursue the path of enlightenment, just as man had.

The stories of these early female monastics show that women were capable of profound spiritual insight, and they helped establish the notion that both women and men can walk the path of the Dhamma equally.
In addition to their personal achievements, these first women of the Sangha played an important role in spreading the Buddha's teachings.
Many of them became teachers in their own right.
They created a rich tradition of monastic life for women, and their wisdom continues to inspire generations of practitioners.
The nuns, or bhikkhuni as they were called, were ordinary women, just like us, with families, social struggles, desires.
What's remarkable is that despite these worldly entanglements, they attain profound states of peace and wisdom.
They too experience the deep release that comes from insight into the nature of suffering and the cessation of suffering, just as the Buddha did.
The poems they wrote show us that the path of awakening is not reserved for any particular gender or group.
The Buddha's teachings can be applied universally, and the Therigata, the songs of the, the poems of the elder nuns, stand as an embodiment of this truth.
These teachings are timeless.
Although the nuns lived over 2,500 years ago, their experiences are profoundly relevant today.
We live in a world filled with distractions, desires, and attachments.
Like the nuns, we often find ourselves struggling to let go of the things that cause us pain.
The Therigata shows us that the path to liberation is not about escaping from the world, but about seeing the world clearly and realizing its impermanence.
Before I get really into the Therigata, I need to tell you a disclaimer.
This was 2,500 years ago.
They were probably composed over the time shortly after the Buddha's life.
But there's a difference between the Therigata and the Theragata.
The women still kind of got the short end of the stick.
There was not much about them or their lives in most cases.
The verses lack historical context.
Even if they are related to an important Buddhist teacher, we are not quite sure what the whole story was.
So take it with a grain of salt like everything else.
All right.
Therigata, the verses of the elder nuns, preserve the voices of these first women of the Sangha who shared the direct experience of the path to enlightenment.
We can find teachings, struggles, and insights of these nuns who transformed their lives through the Buddha Dharma.
It is a collection of poems which is part of the Kodaka Nikaya, which is part of the Pali Canon.
There were 73 verses.
It stands out as one of the earliest records we have of the voices of women in Buddhist history.
It offers a profound insight into their path of awakening.
The verses are filled with vivid depictions of their lives, their inner lives, their challenges, and the joy they experienced upon achieving liberation.
Their words echo down the centuries as a testament to the transformative power of the Dharma, irrespective of gender, status, or social expectations.
There are several themes in the Therigata.
The struggle of liberation from attachment.
I'm going to check the time really quick.
This got longer than I thought.
So, themes in the Therigata.
The struggle to liberate from attachment.
This is a recurring theme.
Their attachment to people, desires, one's own sense of identity.
The liberation can only come when we release all these attachments.
Many of the nuns reflect on their past lives and difficulty they faced in relinquishing worldly concerns.
Take, for example, the verse of Bhikkhuni Kema, one of the most well-known figures in the Therigata.
Kema was a beautiful woman, highly admired for her appearance.
At first, she struggled to see the impermanence of her beauty.
After hearing a discourse by the Buddha, she came to understand how her attachment to her own beauty was a source of suffering.
In her poem, she says,
*I was born in a place of suffering, yet I have gone beyond that suffering.
No longer do I seek after things that fade.
I have crossed over to the other shore.*
Kema realized that her beauty, like all things, is impermanent, which led her to abandon her attachment.
Another theme is the power of wisdom and insight.
The Therigata also emphasizes the transformative power of wisdom, prajna, and insight.
Many nuns speak of the moment when they gained insight into the true nature of suffering and the path to its cessation, leading to the liberation.
Bikkhuni Visakha, another important figure in the Therigata, expresses the deep wisdom she gained from her practice.
Visakha was renowned for her intelligence and teaching.
In her verse, she reflects on the breakthrough that led to her awakening.
*I sought for peace, and peace was found.
When I saw the truth, I became free.
The roots of suffering are destroyed, and I am liberated, never to return.*
Another theme is the joy of awakening.
The nuns express joy and peace upon their enlightenment.
The poems are filled with vivid descriptions of the bliss they experienced when they realized the end of their suffering.
Bikkhuni Upalavana, known for her beauty and wisdom, captures the moment of awakening in her verse.
She says,
*I have crossed over.
I am free.
I have gone beyond.
I have gone beyond.
The path of freedom is now my home.
My heart is at peace, untouched by sorrow.*
Upalavana's expression of being free and having gone beyond reflects profound inner peace that comes from the cessation of craving and attachments.
This joy is not a temporary happiness.
It's not giddiness, but a deep, unshakable peace that comes from understanding the impermanence of things.
Bikkhuni Dhammadhina reflects on the impermanence of the world and the wisdom she gained.
*I have seen the world as it is, shifting, changing, subject to decay.
I let go of the transient, and in letting go, I found peace.*
Like Dhammadhina, our peace, too, lies in not denying the world, but accepting it with its impermanence and learning not to cling to it.
We are all able to attain this peace, whether we are monastics or lay practitioners.
The path of the nuns is open to us all, and let's get rid of the gender.
The path is open to us all.

The women who wrote the poems of the Terigata were just like us, and for the men, I can assure you, there is a counterpart, much bigger and nicer, in front of the Terigata, and it's called the Teragata, the poems of the elder monks.
These women faced their own struggles.
Some were married, some had children, some came from powerful families, yet they each realized that true freedom could not be found in their former circumstances.
Another poem about breakthrough, from the Bhikkhuni Soma.
*I was like a bird in a cage, trapped by desire, trapped by self, but when the cage was opened by wisdom, I flew free, leaving the world behind.*
We actually have a little bit more time, and I would like to read you some of the poems.
I'm going to start with my favorite, which is called Sona, Mother of Ten.
It has my favorite line in it.
*Ten children I bore from this physical heap.
Then, weak from that, aged, I went to a nun.
She taught me the dharma, aggregates, sense spheres, and elements.
Hearing her dharma, I cut off my hair and ordained.*
*Having purified the divine eye, while still a probationer, I know my previous lives, where I lived in the past.
I developed a seamless meditation, well-focused oneness.
I gained the liberation of immediacy from lack of clinging unbound.
The five aggregates, comprehended, stand like a tree, with its root cut through.
I spit on old age.
There is no further becoming.*
I spit on old age.
Not because I think it's not cool, but because there is this judgment that goes along with aging women being useless.
It's over.
This nun saw through that, and she saw that she carried her youth, and she carried her old age, and everything in between.
Let's read Patakara's poem.
*I thought, plowing the field with plows, sowing the ground with seed, supporting their wives and children, young men gather up wealth.
So why is it that I, consummate in virtue, the doer of the teacher's bidding, don't gain unbinding?*
*I'm not lazy or proud.
Washing my feet, I noticed the water, and in watching it flow from high to low, my heart was composed like a fine, thoroughbred steed.
Then, taking a lamp, I entered the hut, checked the bedding, sat down on the bed, and taking a pin, I pulled out the wick, like the flames unbinding was the liberation of awareness.*
One last one.
Kanda, the beggar.
*Before, I had fallen on evil times.
No husband, no children, no relatives, friends, no way to obtain clothing and food.
So, taking a staff and bowl in hand, begging for alms from house to house, feverish from the cold and heat, no way to obtain clothing and food.
Then, seeing a nun, obtaining food and drink, I approached her and said, let me go forth into homelessness.
She, Patakara, from sympathy, let me go forth.
Then, exhorting me, urged me to the highest goal.
Hearing her words, I did her bidding.
Her exhortation was not in vain.
In doubt was the three knowledges, I'm effluent free.*
Effluent free means no more outflow, no more karma being generated.
So that was the introduction into the Therigata, and next week I will also give the Dharma talk and tell you a little bit more about those nuns.
Thank you so very much.
*May our intention in equally extend to every being and place, with the true merit of Buddha's way.
Beings are numberless, I vow to save them.
Delusions are inexhaustible, I vow to end them.
Dharma gates are boundless, I vow to end them.
Buddha's way is unsurpassable, I vow to become it.*

Then, seeing a nun, obtaining food and drink, I approached her and said, let me go forth into homelessness. She, Patakara, from sympathy, let me go forth. Then, exhorting me, urged me to the highest goal. Hearing her words, I did her bidding. Her exhortation was not in vain. In doubt was the three knowledges, I'm effluent free. Effluent free means no more outflow, no more karma being generated. So that was the introduction into the Therigata, and next week I will also give the Dharma talk and tell you a little bit more about those nuns. Thank you so very much.

May our intention in equally extend to every being and place, with the true merit of Buddha's way. Beings are numberless, I vow to save them. Delusions are inexhaustible, I vow to end them. Dharma gates are boundless, I vow to end them. Buddha's way is unsurpassable, I vow to become it.
